entries.question: A permanent is an enchantment with a static ability saying it isn't a creature as long as your devotion to its color is less than five, and your devotion is currently two. A second enchantment then resolves whose static ability says every non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Is the first permanent a creature, and if so what are its power and toughness?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the later timestamped layer‑4 type‑change makes it a creature and the layer‑7b P/T‑setting effect gives it power and toughness equal to its mana value.
entries.answer:
Yes — the first enchantment is a creature, and its power and toughness are each equal to its mana value.

Why: Both static abilities are type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 (the layer where card types are set), and within a layer they're applied in timestamp order [613.6]. The second enchantment's ability entered later, so its "each non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature" effect is applied after the first enchantment's "isn't a creature" effect and overrides it. Note that the first enchantment's ability is a static ability that only states a quality/type conditionally; it is not a characteristic-defining ability, since it sets the value only if a condition is met [604.3a], so it doesn't get any special priority.

Devotion: your devotion to a color is the number of mana symbols of that color among the mana costs of permanents you control, and it is calculated after copy, control, and text-changing effects but before other characteristic-modifying effects [700.5a]. With devotion two (less than five), the first enchantment's own ability is switched "on," but as explained above the later type-changing effect still wins. (If devotion were five or more, the first ability would simply do nothing anyway.)

Power and toughness: while it wasn't a creature it had no power or toughness even though numbers are printed on the card, but a P/T-setting effect still applies to it once it becomes a creature [208.3, 208.3a]. The second enchantment's "power and toughness each equal to its mana value" is a setting effect applied in layer 7b [613.4b], and the parts of an effect apply in their own layers even though the type change happened in layer 4 [613.6]. So if the first enchantment's mana cost is, say, {3}{R} (mana value 4), it is a 4/4 enchantment creature. Any later +N/+N effects would then be added in layer 7c on top of that.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the second enchantment resolved after the first was already on the battlefield, giving it the later timestamp. If the first enchantment had instead entered after the second, the first's "isn't a creature" effect would have the later timestamp and would apply last, leaving it a noncreature enchantment with no power or toughness while your devotion is two.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of opponents — devotion counts only permanents you control — so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.
entries.answer_gold: Yes, it is a creature, and its power and toughness are each equal to its mana value. Both type-changing effects apply in layer 4 and neither depends on the other, so they are applied in timestamp order (CR 613.1d, 613.7): the permanent's own effect removes the creature type first, then the later effect makes it a creature. The power/toughness-setting effect applies in layer 7b (CR 613.4b), after the type has already been settled.

entries.question: You control a 2/2 creature with no abilities, and a permanent whose static ability says creatures with no abilities get +2/+2. A spell resolves giving that creature +1/+0 and first strike until end of turn. An opponent then resolves a permanent whose static ability says creatures they control have first strike and creatures you control can't have first strike. What are your creature's final power and toughness?
entries.reason: Both conclude the opponent's "can't have first strike" prevents the grant so the creature ends without abilities and receives +2/+2 plus +1/+0, making it 5/4.
entries.answer:
Your creature ends up 5/4.

Working it through in layer 7 (all power/toughness changes happen in layer 7, applied in sublayers, and the game recalculates continuously — [613.1g], [613.5], [302.4c]):

1. Base printed values: 2/2.
2. Does the Muraganda-style effect ("creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") apply? A creature that has been *granted* an ability by an effect does have an ability and would not qualify ([113.12], which uses exactly this Muraganda Petroglyphs example). Here, though, the opponent's permanent says creatures you control can't have first strike. That prohibition means the grant of first strike never actually gives your creature the ability, so your creature still has no abilities and does qualify for +2/+2. (Note the pump part of the spell, "+1/+0," is not an ability the creature has — it's an external continuous effect modifying power, applied in layer 7c per [613.4c] — so it doesn't disqualify the creature either.)
3. Layer 7c, in timestamp order: +1/+0 from the spell and +2/+2 from the static ability. 2/2 → 3/2 → 5/4. Order within 7c doesn't matter here since both merely modify ([613.4c]).

No characteristic-defining ability or setting effect is involved, so layers 7a, 7b, and 7d ([613.4a], [613.4b], [613.4d]) are empty here; base power/toughness stays 2/2 ([208.4b]).

Timing note: I'm assuming the opponent's permanent resolved after the spell, as stated. If instead the opponent's permanent had already been on the battlefield when the spell resolved, the result is the same — your creature still never has first strike, so it still counts as having no abilities and is still 5/4. Also note that the +1/+0 and the first-strike grant last only until end of turn; once they wear off, your creature is 2/2 + 2/+2 = 4/4 as long as the +2/+2 permanent remains and the creature still has no abilities.

Multiplayer: this works identically with two players or more than two — the opponent's static ability affects creatures you control regardless of the number of players, and if several opponents controlled such prohibitions the result would be unchanged. The provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific rule that alters this.

One caveat: the provided context doesn't include a numbered rule spelling out how "can't have [ability]" prohibitions interact with ability grants; the conclusion that your creature ends up with no abilities rests on the general principle in [113.12] about granted abilities being removable/preventable.
entries.answer_gold: 5/4. In layer 6, the opponent's can't-have-first-strike effect prevents the spell from granting first strike to your creature (CR 613.1f), and the opponent's permanent grants your creature nothing, so your creature ends layer 6 with no abilities. In layer 7c it therefore receives +2/+2 from the no-abilities effect, and it still receives +1/+0 from the spell, because that spell's power/toughness part applies in layer 7c independently of whether its ability-granting part took effect.

entries.question: You control a permanent that is both a land with a basic land type and a creature. An opponent resolves an effect saying creatures you control lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1. Can you still tap that permanent for mana of the color its basic land type produces?
entries.reason: Both conclude the intrinsic mana ability from the basic land type is still an ability and is removed by the "lose all abilities" effect, so you cannot tap it for colored mana.
entries.answer:
No — while that effect is applied, you can't tap it for colored mana from its basic land type.

Why: a land with a basic land type has the *intrinsic* mana ability "{T}: Add [mana symbol]" ({W} for Plains, {U} for Islands, {B} for Swamps, {R} for Mountains, {G} for Forests), even if no such text is printed on it [305.6]. That's still an ability of the object, so an effect making creatures you control "lose all abilities" strips it away along with everything else. Type-changing effects are applied in layer 4 and ability-adding/removing effects in layer 6 [613.6], so the land type (and the ability it grants) exists first and is then removed by the lose-all-abilities effect. Tapping the permanent is still possible, but it produces nothing.

Details and caveats:
- The permanent is still a land and still a creature; combining card types doesn't change this, and it remains a permanent on the battlefield [300.2a] [110.4c]. It also keeps its basic land type and any supertypes — losing abilities doesn't change types [205.4b].
- Because it keeps the basic land type, other cards that care about "a Forest/Island/etc." still see it (for example, landwalk-style checks) [702.14e], and effects that ask what mana it "could produce" would find none while it has no mana ability [106.7].
- Timing assumption: I'm assuming the lose-all-abilities effect is already resolved and applies to the permanent at the moment you'd tap it. If instead the permanent gains the basic land type from a later effect that also re-establishes abilities, or the opponent's effect stops applying (e.g., it was "until end of turn"), the intrinsic mana ability comes back automatically from the land type [305.6] [613.6]. Likewise, if you tap it for mana with the ability on the stack — mana abilities resolve immediately — but before the ability-removing effect resolves, you get the mana normally.
- This answer doesn't depend on player count: it's the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since only the opponent's continuous effect and your permanent are involved.
entries.answer_gold: No. The mana ability is intrinsic to the basic land type rather than printed on the permanent (CR 305.6), but it is still an ability, so the lose-all-abilities effect removes it in layer 6 (CR 613.1f).

entries.question: A continuous effect from a static ability says all nonland permanents are legendary. An effect then creates a token that is a copy of a legendary creature on the battlefield, and that copy effect specifies the token is not legendary. Once the token is on the battlefield, is it legendary?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — the token is created without the legendary supertype but the separate continuous effect later adds the legendary supertype, making the token legendary.
entries.answer:
Yes — the token ends up legendary on the battlefield.

Why: copy effects only operate on copiable values, which are the values derived from printed text as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and certain "as ... enters" abilities. Other continuous effects — including type- and supertype-changing effects — are not copied (707.2c). So the exception "the token is not legendary" only removes legendary from the token's copiable values; it does not immunize the token from an outside continuous effect.

The "all nonland permanents are legendary" static ability is a separate continuous effect that is applied in the layer system after copiable values are locked in (613.1, 613.1a, 613.2a, 613.2c — layer 1 produces the copiable values, and later layers apply type/supertype changes). Because that effect applies to all nonland permanents currently on the battlefield, it applies to the token once the token is a nonland permanent there, and one continuous effect can override the result of another (613.9). Gaining the legendary supertype doesn't change the token's card types or subtypes, and it retains any other supertypes (205.4b). As a legendary permanent, the token is then subject to the legend rule (205.4d), so if its name matches another legendary permanent you control, you'll put one into the graveyard.

Side note: if the copied creature's legendary status came only from that same static ability rather than its printed text, it wasn't a copiable value in the first place, and the "except it's not legendary" clause had nothing to strip (707.2c, 707.9c). Either way the outcome is the same.

One caveat on timing: while the token is being created, replacement effects apply before continuous effects that modify its characteristics (701.7b), but that concerns creation-time replacements, not the ongoing static ability — once the token is on the battlefield the static ability applies to it.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since the effect described applies to all nonland permanents.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The copy effect determines the token's copiable values, so the token is created without the legendary supertype. But the 'all nonland permanents are legendary' effect applies in layer 4 to every applicable object on the battlefield regardless of when that object entered (CR 613.1d), so it is applied on top of the copiable values and makes the token legendary.

entries.question: A creature receives a flying counter. Later, an ability resolves that makes it lose flying for as long as that effect lasts. Later still, the creature receives a second flying counter. Then one of the two flying counters is removed from it. Does the creature have flying?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — the remaining flying counter has the later timestamp (updated when the second was placed), so it applies after the lose-flying effect and the creature has flying.
entries.answer:
Yes — the creature has flying.

Why: A flying counter and an effect saying the creature "loses flying" are both applied in layer 6 (ability-adding effects, keyword counters, and ability-removing effects) [613.1f], and within that layer they're ordered by timestamp, with the later one winning [613.7a] [113.10c].

1. First flying counter: it gets a timestamp when it's put on the creature [613.7c]. The creature has flying [702.9c].
2. The loses-flying effect resolves with a later timestamp, so it's applied after the counter and the creature has no flying.
3. The second flying counter is put on. Because the creature already had a counter of that kind, *every* flying counter on it receives a new timestamp identical to the new counter's [613.7c]. Both flying counters now have a timestamp later than the loses-flying effect, so flying is granted after it's removed — the creature has flying.
4. Removing one of the two flying counters doesn't change the remaining counter's timestamp; there's no rule that reverts it to an older timestamp. The remaining flying counter still has the newer timestamp, so it is still applied after the loses-flying effect and the creature still has flying (multiple instances would be redundant anyway) [702.9c].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the events in exactly the order given (counter, then loss effect, then second counter, then removal). If instead the loses-flying effect were generated *after* the second counter was placed, that effect would have the latest timestamp and the creature would not have flying for the duration of that effect.

One caveat: if the effect said the creature "can't have flying" rather than "loses flying," no counter or effect could grant it flying at all, regardless of timestamps [113.11]. This analysis is player-count independent — nothing here depends on the number of players.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Keyword counters and ability-removing effects both apply in layer 6 and are applied in timestamp order (CR 613.1f). When the second flying counter was put on the creature, every flying counter already on it received a new timestamp identical to the new counter's (CR 613.7c), so the one remaining counter has a later timestamp than the lose-flying effect and is applied after it.

entries.question: An Equipment is attached to a creature, and its static ability says the equipped creature loses flying. An Aura is then attached to that same creature, and its static ability says the enchanted creature has flying. Does the creature have flying?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: both effects are applied in layer 6 and the later timestamp (the Aura attached last) wins, so the creature has flying.
entries.answer:
Yes — the creature has flying.

Both effects apply in the same layer (ability-adding/removing) and neither depends on the other: nothing about the Equipment's "equipped creature loses flying" changes what the Aura's "enchanted creature has flying" applies to or does, and vice versa [613.8a]. So they're applied in timestamp order, and the later one wins [613.7a] [613.9]. Since the Aura became attached to the creature after the Equipment was already attached, the Aura's effect has the later timestamp and "wins" — the creature has flying. Rule 113.10c states the same general principle: when effects add and remove the same ability, the most recent one prevails.

A couple of clarifications:
- A continuous effect from a static ability isn't "locked in"; it applies to whatever the text currently indicates, so the Equipment's effect is still live — it's just applied before the Aura's [611.3a]. If the Aura leaves or is moved to another creature, its effect stops applying to this creature and the Equipment's "loses flying" is once again the last word, so the creature would lose flying [604.4].
- This is different from the Rune of Flight / Colossus Hammer example in 613.7a, where the Aura enchants the Equipment rather than the creature; there the granted ability shares the Aura's timestamp but the ordering is computed on the Equipment's two abilities [613.7a].
- If the Equipment instead said the creature "can't have flying," the answer would flip: such an effect prevents the ability from being added at all, regardless of timestamps [113.11].

None of this depends on the number of players — the layer/timestamp rules work identically in two-player and multiplayer games. Timing assumption: I'm taking the Equipment as attached first and the Aura attached strictly later, as stated. If the attachments happened in the other order (Aura first, Equipment later), the Equipment's "loses flying" would have the later timestamp and the creature would not have flying.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Both effects apply in layer 6, and neither changes what the other applies to or does, so there is no dependency and they are applied in timestamp order (CR 613.3, 613.7). An Aura or Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached (CR 613.7e), and the Aura was attached later, so its effect is applied last and wins.

entries.question: A permanent's static ability says all creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1. A spell then resolves that puts a creature onto the battlefield and gives that creature haste until end of turn. Does that creature have haste?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the effects are applied in layer 6 and, by timestamp order, the haste-granting effect from the resolved spell is later and so the creature retains haste.
entries.answer:
Yes — the creature has haste. Both effects apply in layer 6 (ability‑adding and ability‑removing effects are applied together there, per rule 613.1f). The permanent's static ability removing all abilities and the spell's effect granting haste are both continuous effects in that layer, and when two effects add and remove the same ability, the most recent one generally prevails (rule 113.10c). Since the spell resolved after the static ability's effect already existed, the haste‑granting effect has the later timestamp and wins, so the creature has haste until end of turn.

A few clarifications:

- Haste means the creature ignores the "summoning sickness" rule: it can attack and can use activated abilities with {T} or {Q} in their costs even though its controller hasn't controlled it continuously since their most recent turn began (rules 702.10a, 702.10c, and the Haste keyword entry).
- Everything else about the static ability still applies: the creature is still base 1/1 (that's a power/toughness‑setting effect in a different layer, not an ability), and any other abilities it printed are still gone.
- Timing matters in one respect: the ability‑removal applies the moment the creature is on the battlefield, so any enters‑the‑battlefield triggered ability it printed will not trigger (rule 603.6b), even though it ends up with haste afterward. Haste itself isn't a trigger, so it's unaffected.
- If instead the permanent said creatures "can't have haste," the answer flips: a can't‑have effect means the haste‑granting part of the resolving spell simply doesn't apply, regardless of timestamps (rule 113.11), while the rest of that spell's effects still work.
- If, hypothetically, the ability‑removing effect were the later one (for example, that permanent entered after the haste was granted), the removal would prevail and the creature would lose haste (rule 113.10c).

None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two‑player game and at a multiplayer table.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Both effects apply in layer 6 and are applied in timestamp order (CR 613.1f, 613.7). The spell's effect was created when it resolved, so it has the later timestamp and is applied after the lose-all-abilities effect, which means the granted haste is not stripped.

entries.question: A creature has a static ability making all cards and permanents a single chosen color. An opponent then resolves an enchantment whose static ability says all creatures lose all abilities. What color is the creature, and what color is the opponent's enchantment?
entries.reason: The candidate reached the opposite conclusion — it incorrectly says the color-setting static ability disappears when abilities are removed, but rule layers make the color-change apply in layer 5 before abilities are removed in layer 6, so the chosen color persists for both objects.
entries.answer:
Once the opponent's enchantment resolves, the creature is its own normal color (the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, or colorless if it has none), and the opponent's enchantment is likewise its own printed color. The chosen color no longer applies to anything.

Why: a static ability generates a continuous effect only for as long as the object actually has that ability. Ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 [613.1f]. The enchantment's "all creatures lose all abilities" applies to the creature (the enchantment itself is not a creature, so it keeps its own ability), stripping the creature of its color-setting static ability. With that ability gone, there is no longer any effect making all cards and permanents the chosen color, so colors revert to the objects' own: an object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost unless an effect changes it [202.2f], [105.3].

Note the ordering logic: this isn't simply "latest timestamp wins" between two color effects — one effect's result determines whether the other effect exists at all, which is exactly the situation described in [613.9]. The color-changing ability can't protect itself here, because making the enchantment a chosen color doesn't remove or alter the enchantment's ability-removing static ability; setting a characteristic like color is not the same as granting or removing an ability [113.12].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the color-changing creature was already on the battlefield when the enchantment resolved. The result is the same in the other order — the moment the enchantment is on the battlefield, the creature has no abilities, so it never sets any colors. If the enchantment somehow leaves the battlefield later, the creature regains its ability and the chosen-color effect resumes.

Multiplayer: this works identically at any number of players; nothing here depends on there being exactly two players. Every player's cards and permanents are affected by the same layer analysis.

One caveat: the provided context does not include the text of layer 5 (color-changing effects) or the dependency rule 613.8 in full, so the layer numbering for the color effect is stated from the general framework in [613.1f] and [613.9] rather than a quoted layer-5 rule.
entries.answer_gold: Both are the chosen color. The color-changing effect applies in layer 5 and the ability-removing effect applies in layer 6 (CR 613.1e, 613.1f). Because layer 5 is applied before layer 6, the color-changing effect has already been applied by the time the ability generating it is removed, and it continues to apply. The effect applies to all permanents, so the opponent's enchantment is that color too.
